title: Coagulation
subtitle: INR, PT, APTT, fibrinogen and DIC patterns
summary: INR, PT, APTT, fibrinogen and DIC patterns
introduction: Interpret INR/PT/APTT with indication, anticoagulant, dose timing, liver function, platelet count, fibrinogen and bleeding. INR is designed mainly to monitor warfarin and is not a universal measure of bleeding risk.

rows.name: INR / PT
rows.referenceRange: INR about 0.8–1.2 when not anticoagulated; warfarin target commonly 2.0–3.0 but indication-specific
notes: Raised by warfarin, vitamin K deficiency, liver synthetic dysfunction, DIC or factor deficiency. Direct oral anticoagulants can alter PT/INR unpredictably; a normal INR does not exclude a clinically relevant DOAC effect.

rows.name: APTT
notes: Prolonged with unfractionated heparin, factor deficiencies/inhibitors, lupus anticoagulant or DIC. A normal APTT does not reliably exclude DOAC activity.

rows.name: Fibrinogen
notes: Low fibrinogen with prolonged PT/APTT, thrombocytopenia and bleeding supports consumption such as DIC. It can be normal or raised early because it is also an acute-phase protein.

rows.name: Possible DIC
notes: Look for falling platelets, prolonged PT and APTT, low fibrinogen, raised D-dimer, bleeding/oozing, purpura, organ dysfunction and a trigger such as sepsis, trauma, malignancy or obstetric catastrophe.

urgentFindings: Any anticoagulated patient with intracranial symptoms, haemodynamic compromise, haematemesis, melaena, major haematuria or uncontrolled bleeding.
Markedly raised INR with bleeding, or INR ≥8 even without bleeding: follow the local warfarin reversal pathway.
Possible DIC with bleeding, shock, mottling, falling platelets or organ dysfunction.
Do not delay emergency treatment because PT/APTT/INR are normal when a DOAC was taken recently.
overrides: Use the reporting laboratory’s reference ranges and compare with previous results, symptoms, observations, medication and fluid status.

commonPatterns.title: Warfarin over-anticoagulation
findings: INR above the patient's target therapeutic range
interpretation: Bleeding risk rises with the degree of INR elevation, and further with intercurrent illness, interacting medicines, dietary vitamin K changes or missed monitoring
A markedly raised INR can occur without bleeding but still carries significant risk
actions: Ask about bleeding, recent dose changes, missed monitoring, antibiotics, diet and alcohol
Follow the local warfarin reversal pathway if INR is markedly raised, and treat any bleeding as time-critical (see urgent findings)
Arrange medical review for dose adjustment and a plan for repeat INR monitoring

commonPatterns.title: Possible liver synthetic dysfunction
findings: Not explained by warfarin or another anticoagulant
Known or suspected liver disease, or deranged liver blood tests
interpretation: The liver synthesises most clotting factors, so synthetic dysfunction (chronic liver disease or acute liver failure) can prolong PT/INR even without anticoagulant use
Unlike warfarin, this coagulopathy cannot be reliably reversed with vitamin K alone if synthetic failure is advanced
actions: Review medication history to exclude an anticoagulant or vitamin K antagonist effect
Request liver blood tests and correlate with jaundice, ascites, encephalopathy or known chronic liver disease (see further testing)
Arrange medical review; treat as urgent if there is bleeding, encephalopathy or acute liver failure is suspected

commonPatterns.title: Vitamin K deficiency / malabsorption picture
findings: APTT usually normal or only mildly affected
Poor nutritional intake, malabsorption, prolonged antibiotic use, or obstructive jaundice
interpretation: Vitamin K is needed to synthesise several clotting factors; deficiency from malabsorption, malnutrition, biliary obstruction or broad-spectrum antibiotics can prolong PT/INR in a pattern similar to early warfarin effect
actions: Ask about diet, alcohol use, recent antibiotics, biliary symptoms and malabsorptive conditions
Request liver blood tests to help distinguish this from synthetic liver dysfunction (see further testing)
Arrange medical review for consideration of vitamin K replacement and investigation of the underlying cause

commonPatterns.title: Isolated prolonged APTT
findings: No clinical bleeding, or bleeding out of proportion to the result
interpretation: Consider unfractionated heparin effect, a factor VIII/IX/XI deficiency (including haemophilia), lupus anticoagulant, or a sample/collection artefact
An isolated prolonged APTT without bleeding is not automatically reassuring — lupus anticoagulant can prolong APTT while actually increasing thrombotic risk
actions: Check for heparin (including flushes/lines) and recent sample handling before assuming a true factor abnormality
Ask about personal or family bleeding history and any history of thrombosis
Arrange medical review for further specialist testing (mixing studies, factor assays) rather than acting on this result alone

commonPatterns.title: Possible DIC (composite picture)
findings: A recognised trigger: sepsis, major trauma, malignancy or obstetric catastrophe
interpretation: This combination, especially with bleeding/oozing, purpura or organ dysfunction, supports disseminated intravascular coagulation rather than a single-factor problem
Fibrinogen can be normal or even raised early because it is also an acute-phase protein, so a 'normal' fibrinogen does not exclude evolving DIC
actions: Treat as time-critical if bleeding, shock, mottling or organ dysfunction is present (see urgent findings)
Request FBC and D-dimer to support the picture, and treat the underlying trigger urgently (see further testing)
Arrange urgent senior/medical review — DIC management depends on the driving cause

commonPatterns.title: DOAC effect on coagulation screen
findings: Patient taking a direct oral anticoagulant (e.g. apixaban, rivaroxaban, dabigatran, edoxaban)
PT/APTT/INR normal, mildly abnormal, or unexpectedly abnormal
interpretation: DOACs affect PT/APTT/INR unpredictably depending on the specific drug and assay used locally — a normal screen does not exclude a clinically relevant anticoagulant effect, and an abnormal screen does not reliably quantify it
actions: Establish the specific DOAC, dose, timing of last dose and renal function, as these determine bleeding risk more than the coagulation screen
Do not delay emergency treatment for bleeding or suspected intracranial haemorrhage while awaiting a specific anticoagulant assay (see urgent findings)
Discuss with senior/specialist advice if a specific anti-Xa or drug level assay is needed (see further testing)

rationale: Supports identification of DIC when combined with a falling platelet count, prolonged PT/APTT and low fibrinogen
Also relevant to VTE risk assessment where clinically indicated, interpreted alongside pre-test probability
Helps distinguish liver synthetic dysfunction from vitamin K deficiency or an isolated anticoagulant effect as the cause of a prolonged PT/INR
Platelet count is essential context for bleeding risk alongside PT/APTT, and a falling platelet count supports a DIC or consumptive picture

furtherTesting.test: Anti-Xa assay or specific DOAC level
rationale: Gives a more specific measure of anticoagulant effect than PT/APTT when heparin or a DOAC level needs to be quantified, for example before urgent surgery or when bleeding is disproportionate to the routine screen
Specialist tests to distinguish a factor deficiency from an inhibitor (e.g. lupus anticoagulant) when PT or APTT is unexpectedly and persistently prolonged
A single result can reflect sampling artefact (e.g. under-filled citrate tube, delayed processing); repeating confirms a genuine abnormality before escalating or reversing anticoagulation

specimens.notes: Whole blood — blue-top sodium-citrate tube. Fill exactly to the tube's fill line — under- or overfilling changes the blood:citrate ratio and invalidates PT/APTT/INR.
